title.en: Language work for Carrier of Words: metaphors, alliteration, present perfect, passive voice and word maps

text.en: Postman Khetaram trudges across scorching Thar dunes in Carrier of Words, delivering letters to remote families. The chapter turns his desert endurance into rich metaphors, teaches how present perfect expresses seven different time shades, and shows how active verbs become passive.

Notice four vivid phrases in Khetaram's story: 'crumbles into sand' means disappears in the desert; 'turn into a trickle before drying out' means shrink gradually until stopping completely.
Similarly, 'give a new lease of life' means grant a fresh chance to continue, while 'bearing words across this desolate geography' describes carrying letters through barren, sparsely populated terrain.
Identify two poetic devices in 'his only protection against the desert's furies, the scorching summer winds and swirling sandstorms which turn him into a walking sandman'.
First, 'scorching summer' and 'swirling sandstorms' repeat the starting /s/ consonant sound—that musical repetition of initial sounds is alliteration.
Second, 'desert's furies' personifies desert storms as fierce anger, while calling Khetaram 'a walking sandman' compares him directly to a sand statue without 'like'—making it a metaphor.
Match Unit 7 context words precisely: 'arid farmland' suggests dry soil with low yield, 'concessional' points to lower interest rates for farmers, 'desolate' evokes vast emptiness, and 'gaunt' pictures a thin farmer awaiting rain.
Now explore seven distinct functions of present perfect tense (has/have + past participle): finished actions with present results ('She has found her book') and recent events ('I have just eaten').
Other present perfect functions include life experience ('Have you ever seen a play?'), personal accomplishment ('I have finished my project'), gradual change ('become a good bowler in five years'), repeated events, and continuing periods ('studied here for six years').
Practising the stamp-collection fill-in: 'I have just got a collection', 'He has collected these stamps', 'I have studied', 'I have begun', and 'Grandfather has truly inspired me'.
Next contrast voice using postal work. In 'GDS delivers the mail at the border', the subject (GDS) performs the action, so the verb is in active voice.
In 'The mail is delivered by the GDS at the border', the receiver ('the mail') becomes the grammatical subject, and the verb uses 'be + past participle'—that is passive voice.
Notice when converting active to passive: choose passive voice whenever the action or recipient ('the mail', 'a parcel') matters more than naming who did it every time.
In 'Words', figurative lines carry clear lessons: 'satisfy the heart' means make happy, 'depart and leave but empty air' means leave no lasting effect, and 'hosts of words' means countless words.
Finally, the poem teaches building Word Maps: for every word like 'cheer' or 'depart', list its meaning in your own words, synonyms, antonyms, a sentence, and a visual symbol.

problem.en: Change to passive voice and name the poetic device: (a) Postmen sort hundreds of letters every morning. (b) 'swirling sandstorms'

text.en: (a) Hundreds of letters are sorted by postmen every morning.

why.en: Object 'hundreds of letters' moves to subject position, paired with plural 'are' + past participle 'sorted'.
Both nearby words begin with the same /s/ sound.

prompt.en: Contrast active and passive voice using a sentence about mail delivery, and list the five parts of a Unit 7 Word Map.

requiredIdeas.en: Active voice puts the doer as subject (GDS delivers the mail); passive puts the receiver first using be + past participle (The mail is delivered by the GDS)
Word Map includes: meaning in own words, synonyms, antonyms, an example sentence, and a quick sketch/symbol
Alliteration repeats initial sounds; metaphor directly identifies two unlike things

commonMisconceptions.en: Forgetting the form of 'be' (is/are/was) in passive verbs

points.en: Alliteration repeats initial consonant sounds (swirling sandstorms); metaphor equates two things directly (a walking sandman).
Present perfect (has/have + past participle) covers recent acts, experiences, achievements, changes over time and ongoing spans.
Active voice highlights who acts; passive voice (be + past participle) highlights who or what receives the action.
Word Maps deepen vocabulary by linking meaning, synonyms, antonyms, a sentence and a symbol.
